abstract: Forecasting future world events is a challenging but valuable task. Forecasts of climate, geopolitical conflict, pandemics and economic indicators help shape policy and decision making. In these domains, the judgment of expert humans contributes to the best forecasts. Given advances in language modeling, can these forecasts be automated? To this end, we introduce Autocast, a dataset containing thousands of forecasting questions and an accompanying news corpus. Questions are taken from forecasting tournaments, ensuring high quality, real-world importance, and diversity. The news corpus is organized by date, allowing us to precisely simulate the conditions under which humans made past forecasts (avoiding leakage from the future). Motivated by the difficulty of forecasting numbers across orders of magnitude (e.g. global cases of COVID-19 in 2022), we also curate IntervalQA, a dataset of numerical questions and metrics for calibration. We test language models on our forecasting task and find that performance is far below a human expert baseline. However, performance improves with increased model size and incorporation of relevant information from the news corpus. In sum, Autocast poses a novel challenge for large language models and improved performance could bring large practical benefits.

summary.idea: Autocast pairs thousands of tournament forecasting questions with a date-organized news corpus. IntervalQA separately tests numerical questions and calibration when answers span very different scales.
summary.limitations: The abstract reports no detailed forecast scores or evidence of expert-level performance. Historical evaluation with dated news also does not by itself establish reliability for future policy or economic decisions.
summary.problem: Forecasting world events requires using incomplete evidence available before outcomes are known. Language-model evaluations need realistic questions and careful protection against future-information leakage.
summary.results: Evaluated language models perform far below expert humans, but larger models and relevant retrieved news improve forecasts. The datasets establish a challenging benchmark for automated event prediction.
summary.tldr: Benchmark language-model forecasting with time-appropriate evidence and compare it directly with human expertise.

title: Forecasting Future World Events With Neural Networks

abstract: Adding additional guidance to pretrained diffusion models has become an increasingly popular research area, with extensive applications in computer vision, reinforcement learning, and AI for science. Recently, several studies have proposed training-free loss-based guidance by using off-the-shelf networks pretrained on clean images. This approach enables zero-shot conditional generation for universal control formats, which appears to offer a free lunch in diffusion guidance. In this paper, we aim to develop a deeper understanding of training-free guidance, as well as overcome its limitations. We offer a theoretical analysis that supports training-free guidance from the perspective of optimization, distinguishing it from classifier-based (or classifier-free) guidance. To elucidate their drawbacks, we theoretically demonstrate that training-free guidance is more susceptible to misaligned gradients and exhibits slower convergence rates compared to classifier guidance. We then introduce a collection of techniques designed to overcome the limitations, accompanied by theoretical rationale and empirical evidence. Our experiments in image and motion generation confirm the efficacy of these techniques.

summary.idea: The paper interprets training-free guidance as optimization and compares its behavior with classifier-based guidance. It then introduces techniques motivated by the identified gradient-alignment and convergence problems.
summary.limitations: The abstract does not describe the individual corrective techniques, numerical gains, or all assumptions behind the comparison. It therefore does not establish that every external loss can guide every pretrained diffusion model effectively.
summary.problem: A pretrained diffusion model can be guided by an external loss without retraining, but the resulting gradients may not steer generation reliably. The reason for this weakness needs clearer analysis.
summary.results: The theory shows greater susceptibility to misaligned gradients and slower convergence for training-free guidance. Image- and motion-generation experiments support the proposed improvements.
summary.tldr: Explain why training-free diffusion guidance can struggle, then improve it using the resulting optimization insights.

title: Understanding and Improving Training-free Loss-based Diffusion Guidance
